newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Tutu urges S.Africans to beat amnesty deadline.
newsitem.headline: Tutu urges S.Africans to beat amnesty deadline.

text.p: Archbishop Desmond Tutu on Monday urged participants in the apartheid war to apply for amnesty before the deadline expires in six days, calling his truth commission South Africa's last chance to heal the past.

"Our political leaders will be squandering an important opportunity for putting the past behind them if they do not come forward and participate in the amnesty process," Tutu, chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, said in a statement.

"There is no instrument with the same potential for ending the accusations and counter-accusations, the recriminations and political bickering which will plague this country for generations to come, if you do not seize the opportunity," he said.
Those who do not apply for amnesty by the December 14 deadline stand to be charged in court if evidence emerges that they committed a crime.

The truth commission, set up last year to unveil as much as possible of the dirty war between white minority governments and black liberation groups, has the power to grant indemnity from prosecution to those who confess their deeds fully.

Defence Minister Joe Modise, who led the armed wing of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress for more than two decades , has said he intends to apply for amnesty but few leaders of previous apartheid governments have done so.

The two surviving white former presidents, P.W. Botha and F.W. de Klerk, have both said they see no need to apply. Former defence minister Magnus Malan and Winnie Mandela, divorced wife of President Mandela, have also ruled out applying.
Tutu said in his statement there was confusion about who needed to request amnesty.

"We can say to individuals they should apply if they have done something which might result in a prosecution or a civil action for damages," he said. "People who do not apply for amnesty do so at their own peril."
Tutu said those who applied did not have to acknowledge they had acted wrongly.
"Indeed, you are able to tell the amnesty committee that you are proud of what you did...There is no requirement that amnesty applicants should express remorse."

The amnesty provision was intended to encourage protagonists in South Africa's race war to come forward voluntarily with information, but Tutu added: "We are hopeful that we will get to a substantial part of the truth, including identifying key figures, even without amnesty applications."
